title: An AI-written proof narrows where the zeta zeros can hide; Riemann’s line stays unproven
body: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI posted 722 mathematics manuscripts to a [public repository](https://github.com/openai/math), and one claims the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, [Quanta Magazine reported](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-proved-the-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-what-happens-now-20261019/). The Riemann zeta function, 1 + 1/2ˢ + 1/3ˢ + …, equals a product with one factor per prime, so the points where it vanishes control how the primes are spread; those zeros lie in a strip with real part between 0 and 1, and [Riemann’s 1859 conjecture](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/), says they all sit on the middle line, real part ½. The AI’s papers claim less: no zeros beyond 11/12 or below 1/12. A 199-page version proving the looser bounds 1/8 and 7/8 was machine-checked in the Lean proof assistant; the 49-page 11/12 version has not been, and mathematicians reading it think it holds, though Peter Sarnak will not call it a theorem until every detail is checked. The zero furthest from the edge sets how far prime counts can stray, by roughly x to the power θ: up to a billion, about 180 million for 11/12, against about 32,000 if Riemann is right.

slides.question: The Riemann hypothesis says every nontrivial zero of the zeta function has a real part of exactly what?
slides.explanation: One half. The zeros are known to lie in the strip between 0 and 1; Riemann’s 1859 guess puts them all on the middle line. The new AI papers only narrow the strip, to between 1/12 and 11/12.

slides.alt: Animation on chalkboard blue: a stack of manuscripts, the zeta series and Euler’s product, a critical strip with a gold dashed line at ½ and white zeros on it, red walls at 1/12 and 11/12 and green dashed ones at 1/8 and 7/8, and log-scale bars of x to the theta up to a billion.

slides.prompt: Count primes up to a trillion. Slide θ until the error bound falls under 1% of the count. How far below 11/12 must it go?
slides.takeaway: To about 0.71. The 11/12 bound still allows an error near 10% of the prime count up to a trillion, 7/8 about 5%, while Riemann’s ½ would give one millionth. Narrowing the strip helps; only the line makes the bound tiny.

slides.heading: From Riemann to the AI papers

events.text: Bernhard Riemann conjectures that all the zeros have real part ½
Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin: no zeros on the strip’s edges
The Clay Institute makes it a Millennium Prize Problem
OpenAI posts 722 AI manuscripts, one claiming no zeros beyond 11/12

slides.heading: What is checked, what is claimed

left.label: Checked in Lean
left.text: A 199-page version: all zeros have real part between 1/8 and 7/8, verified line by line by the Lean proof assistant, Quanta reports.

right.label: Being read
right.text: A 49-page version: between 1/12 and 11/12. Not machine-checked; experts who read it think it holds. Not a theorem yet, says Peter Sarnak.

slides.question: What would the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, as claimed in October 2026, say about the zeta function’s zeros?
options: They keep away from the strip’s edges
They all sit on the line ½
slides.explanation: No zero has real part beyond 11/12 or below 1/12: the strip where zeros can live shrinks. Riemann’s full hypothesis, every zero on the line ½, remains open.
